name: Opening Portals
description: Pavel plays a famous computer game. A player is responsible for a whole country and he can travel there freely, complete quests and earn experience. This country has n cities connected by m bidirectional roads of different lengths so that it is possible to get from any city to any other one. There are portals in k of these cities. At the beginning of the game all portals are closed. When a player visits a portal city, the portal opens. Strange as it is, one can teleport from an open portal to an open one. The teleportation takes no time and that enables the player to travel quickly between rather remote regions of the country. At the beginning of the game Pavel is in city number 1 . He wants to open all portals as quickly as possible. How much time will he need for that?
input_specification: The first line contains two space-separated integers n and m ( 1 ≤ n ≤ 10 5 , 0 ≤ m ≤ 10 5 ) that show how many cities and roads are in the game. Each of the next m lines contains the description of a road as three space-separated integers x i , y i , w i ( 1 ≤ x i , y i ≤ n , x i ≠ y i , 1 ≤ w i ≤ 10 9 ) — the numbers of the cities connected by the i -th road and the time needed to go from one city to the other one by this road. Any two cities are connected by no more than one road. It is guaranteed that we can get from any city to any other one, moving along the roads of the country. The next line contains integer k ( 1 ≤ k ≤ n ) — the number of portals. The next line contains k space-separated integers p 1 , p 2 , ..., p k — numbers of the cities with installed portals. Each city has no more than one portal.
output_specification: Print a single number — the minimum time a player needs to open all portals. Please, do not use the %lld specifier to read or write 64-bit integers in C++. It is preferred to use the cin , cout streams or the %I64d specifier.
approach_summary: Formulate the state transition graph with non-negative weights. Execute Dijkstra's algorithm with priority queue to find shortest paths in O((V + E) log V).

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 196E — Opening Portals [168. Dijkstra's Algorithm]
topic_editorial.summary: Single-source shortest path using Dijkstra's algorithm.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: Because all edge weights are non-negative, the shortest distance to the unvisited vertex with the minimum tentative distance is finalized and cannot be decreased by further transitions (greedy choice property).
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Graph Modeling
Construct an adjacency list with pairs $(v, w)$ for each directed or undirected edge from $u$ to $v$ with weight $w \ge 0$.

### Step 2: Distance Table Initialization
Initialize $dist[v] = \infty$ for all vertices, with $dist[\text{source}] = 0$.
Push $(0, \text{source})$ into a min-priority queue `std::priority_queue<pair<long long, int>, vector<pair<long long, int>>, greater<>>`.

### Step 3: Relaxation Loop
While the priority queue is not empty:
1. Pop $(d, u)$. If $d > dist[u]$, discard (stale entry).
2. For each neighbor $(v, w)$ of $u$:
   If $dist[u] + w < dist[v]$:
   $$dist[v] = dist[u] + w$$
   Push $(dist[v], v)$ into the priority queue.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((V + E) \log V)$
  Every vertex is extracted from the priority queue at most once. For every edge, we perform at most one priority queue push operation taking $\mathcal{O}(\log V)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(V + E)$
  Required for storing the adjacency list and the distance array.
